## Today

::: {.objectives}
1. What a satellite sensor actually measures
2. The **four resolutions**, and the trade-offs between them
3. Spectral indices: **NDVI**, EVI, NDWI — what they mean and where they fail
4. The main missions and where to get the data
5. **Environmental annotation**: attaching covariates to a trajectory in space
   *and* time
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
A tracking dataset on its own tells you *where*. Remote sensing tells you
*what was there* — and that is what turns a map into ecology.
:::

# 1 · What a sensor measures {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## Radiation, not "pictures"

::: {.incremental}
- The Sun emits across the electromagnetic spectrum; surfaces **reflect**
  some of it and **absorb** the rest
- A passive sensor records the **radiance** arriving at the detector in a set
  of wavelength **bands**
- That raw signal is contaminated by the atmosphere, the Sun's angle, the
  viewing angle and the terrain
- What you download is the result of a **processing chain**, and the level
  matters
:::

. . .

**Level 1** — top of atmosphere radiance/reflectance.
**Level 2** — surface reflectance, atmospherically corrected. *Start here.*
**Level 3+** — derived products: NDVI composites, land cover, LAI.

---

## Why vegetation looks the way it does

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Healthy green vegetation:

- **absorbs** strongly in the **red** (~660 nm) — chlorophyll is doing
  photosynthesis
- **reflects** strongly in the **near infrared** (~850 nm) — the internal leaf
  structure scatters it

So the *contrast* between red and NIR is a measure of green biomass.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.keyidea}
That single fact is the basis of essentially every vegetation index ever
published.
:::
:::
:::

---

## Active sensors

::: {.incremental}
- **Radar (SAR)** — emits microwaves and measures the return. Sees **through
  cloud and at night**. Sentinel-1. Sensitive to structure and moisture, not
  to greenness.
- **LiDAR** — emits laser pulses, measures return time. Gives **3-D
  structure**: canopy height, vertical complexity. GEDI (spaceborne),
  airborne for fine detail.
:::

. . .

For a forest animal, canopy height and vertical structure from LiDAR are often
far more informative than NDVI — greenness saturates in dense forest, but
structure does not.

# 2 · The four resolutions {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## You cannot have all four

::: {.incremental}
- **Spatial** — pixel size. 10 m (Sentinel-2) … 500 m (MODIS) … 25 km (some
  climate products)
- **Temporal** — revisit time. 5 days (Sentinel-2) vs **daily** (MODIS) vs
  16 days (Landsat)
- **Spectral** — number and width of bands. 4 broad bands vs 200 narrow
  (hyperspectral)
- **Radiometric** — bit depth; how finely brightness is quantised
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
They trade off against each other: a detector collecting light from a small
patch, in a narrow band, gets few photons — so it needs a longer dwell time,
which means a narrower swath and a longer revisit.
:::

---

## The missions you will actually use
| Mission | Spatial | Temporal | Since | Good for |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **MODIS** (Terra/Aqua) | 250–500 m | Daily | 2000 | Long consistent NDVI series |
| **VIIRS** | 375–750 m | Daily | 2012 | MODIS successor |
| **Landsat 5/7/8/9** | 30 m | 16 days | **1984** | Long-term landscape change |
| **Sentinel-2** | 10–20 m | 5 days | 2015 | Fine-grained habitat |
| **Sentinel-1** (SAR) | 10 m | 6–12 days | 2014 | Cloud-free, structure, water |
| **GEDI** (LiDAR) | 25 m footprint | sampled | 2019 | Canopy height |

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
**Match the pixel to the animal and to your positional error.** A 10 m
Sentinel pixel is wasted on an Argos fix with 5 km error — and a 500 m MODIS
pixel is useless for a dormouse.
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
You study habitat selection by a forest ungulate using GPS collars (error
~15 m, hourly fixes) in a landscape with small forest patches of 1–5 ha. Which
product for vegetation cover?

- [ ] MODIS NDVI, 250 m, daily
- [x] Sentinel-2, 10–20 m, every 5 days
- [ ] A 1 km global land-cover map
- [ ] Sentinel-1 SAR, 10 m

::: {.quiz-feedback}
A 1–5 ha patch is roughly 100–220 m across. A **250 m MODIS pixel is larger
than the patch**, so every fix would get a mixed value averaging forest and
open land — the very contrast you are trying to measure would be erased. A
1 km product is hopeless for the same reason.

Sentinel-2 at 10–20 m resolves those patches comfortably, and its 5-day
revisit captures the growing season. Its resolution is also well matched to
15 m GPS error: finer would just add noise.

Sentinel-1 is excellent for structure and for cloudy regions, but it does not
measure greenness — it is the right answer to a different question.
:::
:::

# 3 · Spectral indices {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## NDVI

$$\text{NDVI} = \frac{\text{NIR} - \text{Red}}{\text{NIR} + \text{Red}}$$

::: {.incremental}
- Ranges −1 to +1. Water < 0; bare soil/rock ~0.1–0.2; sparse vegetation
  ~0.2–0.4; dense green vegetation 0.6–0.9
- A **proxy** for green biomass and primary productivity
- Normalised, so it partly cancels illumination and viewing-angle effects
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**It saturates.** Above ~0.8 — closed canopy — NDVI stops responding to extra
biomass. In rainforest it is nearly flat and nearly useless.
:::

---

## The other indices worth knowing
| Index | Formula | Use |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **EVI** | $2.5\frac{\text{NIR}-\text{Red}}{\text{NIR}+6\text{Red}-7.5\text{Blue}+1}$ | Like NDVI but resists saturation and soil background |
| **NDWI** | $\frac{\text{Green}-\text{NIR}}{\text{Green}+\text{NIR}}$ | Open water — very useful for waterholes |
| **NDSI** | $\frac{\text{Green}-\text{SWIR}}{\text{Green}+\text{SWIR}}$ | Snow cover |
| **LAI / fPAR** | modelled | Leaf area, absorbed radiation |

---

## Beyond greenness: derived metrics

::: {.incremental}
- **Rate of green-up** (the derivative of NDVI in time) — this, not NDVI
  itself, is what drives the *green wave surfing* of migratory ungulates
- **Phenology metrics** — start of season, peak, length
- **Terrain** from a DEM: slope, aspect, ruggedness, topographic position
- **Distance to** — water, roads, forest edge. Often the strongest predictor
  in the whole model
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
The best covariate is rarely the raw band. It is a transformation that
corresponds to something the animal could plausibly perceive or care about.
:::

# 4 · Annotation {background-color="#14525a"}

---

## The operation

For every fix, look up the environment **there** and **then**.

::: {.incremental}
- **Static** covariates — elevation, slope, distance to river. One raster;
  `extract()` and done.
- **Dynamic** covariates — NDVI, temperature, snow. A **stack** of rasters
  with timestamps. You must match each fix to the right layer.
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
A track that spans two years annotated with a *single* NDVI image is not
annotated — it is decorated. If your covariate varies in time and your
analysis does not, you have thrown away the mechanism.
:::

---

## Doing it in time

```r
# Which layer does each fix belong to?
layer_dates <- as.Date(c("2005-01-01", "2005-01-17", ...))

idx <- findInterval(as.Date(trk$t_), layer_dates)

# Extract from the whole stack, then pick the right column per row
vals <- terra::extract(ndvi_stack, vect(trk))[, -1]
trk$ndvi <- vals[cbind(seq_len(nrow(vals)), idx)]
```

. . .

`Movebank Env-DATA` does this for you, including interpolation in time, for
dozens of products. Use it for real projects — but understand what it is doing
first, which is what today's exercise is for.

---

## Scale is a decision, not a detail

::: {.incremental}
- Do you want the value **at the fix**, or the **mean within a buffer**?
- A buffer radius is a hypothesis about **perceptual range** — how far the
  animal can assess its surroundings
- Different radii can reverse the sign of an effect
:::

. . .

```r
terra::extract(ndvi, vect(trk), buffer = 500, fun = mean)
```

::: {.keyidea}
Choose the radius from biology, before you look at the results. Fitting at
ten radii and reporting the best one is a garden of forking paths.
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
You annotate two years of buffalo fixes with a single dry-season NDVI image
and find a strong positive selection for high NDVI. What is the main problem?

- [ ] NDVI saturates in dense vegetation
- [x] The covariate is static while both the animal and the vegetation varied seasonally
- [ ] The pixel size is too coarse
- [ ] NDVI cannot be used for savanna

::: {.quiz-feedback}
The image describes one moment. Over two years, vegetation in a savanna swings
enormously between wet and dry season, and the buffalo's needs swing with it.
By holding NDVI fixed you have conflated "places that were green **in that dry
season**" with "places that are green **when the animal was there**".

What you have measured is selection for *persistently* productive places —
which may be interesting, but is not what the model claims.

The result can even be the *opposite* sign from the time-matched analysis: an
animal may select the greenest available patch at every moment while showing
no preference for places that are green on average.

Fix: use a time series and match each fix to the contemporaneous layer.
:::
:::

---

## Common failures
::: {.incremental}
- **CRS mismatch** — or worse, passing a bare coordinate matrix (Class 2)
- **Cloud contamination** — an uncomposited optical image over the tropics is
  mostly cloud. Use quality flags; use composites.
- **Fill values** — `-3000` or `32767` read as real numbers will destroy your
  model. Check the product's documentation for the scale factor and no-data value.
- **Scale factors** — MODIS NDVI is stored as integers; multiply by 0.0001
- **Time zones** — your fixes are UTC; is the product local solar time?
:::

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
After every annotation: `summary()` the new column. If the range is
`-3000` to `10000`, you have raw integers, not NDVI.
:::

---

## Quiz

::: {.quiz}
Your GPS fixes have ~15 m error. You have both a 10 m Sentinel-2 product and a
500 m MODIS product. You take the 10 m one because finer is better. When is
that reasoning wrong?

- [ ] Never — finer resolution is always preferable
- [x] When the process you are modelling operates at a coarser scale than the pixel
- [ ] When the file is too large to process
- [ ] Only for aquatic species

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Resolution should match **the scale of the process**, not simply be as fine as
available. If an animal responds to the overall productivity of a valley, a
10 m pixel measures the individual bush it happened to stand next to — real
variation, but not the variation driving the behaviour. You add noise and lose
power.

The two constraints are:

- the pixel should not be much **finer** than your positional error (you
  cannot tell which pixel the animal was in);
- the pixel should not be much **coarser** than the animal's typical
  displacement (Class 8 shows exactly what breaks when it is).

Between those bounds, the choice is a hypothesis about the animal's perceptual
scale — and you should state it.
:::
:::

:::

---

## Recap

::: {.incremental}
- Sensors record **radiance in bands**; products are processed, and the
  processing level matters
- Four resolutions, all trading off. **Match the pixel to the animal and to
  your positional error**
- NDVI is red/NIR contrast: useful, and it **saturates**
- Annotation must match in **space and in time**; a static covariate for a
  dynamic process is a modelling error, not a shortcut
- Buffer radius encodes a hypothesis about perception. Choose it first
:::
